maintopic: THE LATE HON. A. J. BROOKS EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF FORMER MINISTER

speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillel (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. A. J. BROOKS EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF FORMER MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it would be the wish of all hon. members to record in Hansard, the sincere regret of this house on the news of the sudden passing last night of the late Colonel the Hon. Alfred Brooks. Colonel Brooks, a minister of veterans affairs from 1957 to 1960 and a distinguished veteran of both world wars, was regarded by veterans, by his colleagues on all sides of the house and by the staff of the department as one of the staunchest advocates of veterans rights ever to hold the office of minister of that department.
He was also a veteran in another sense, a veteran of public service outside the armed forces. Colonel Brooks was a teacher and a lawyer, skilled in both professions. He served with distinction as an elected representative in the New Brunswick legislature, in this house and in the other place continuously from 1925 until his death.
I am certain all hon. members will wish to join me and the government in extending our most sincere sympathy to Mrs. Brooks and her two sons in their time of sorrow.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE HON. A. J. BROOKS EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF FORMER MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I have the attention of the house for a few minutes to say a few words about the late Senator Brooks. His career was almost unique in the range and variety of service rendered to Canada. As the minister has already indicated, Senator Brooks had a long career of service as a lawyer, teacher and soldier and was
responsible for the interests of his fellow veterans as a member of the federal government. He had a distinguished career in the legislature of New Brunswick and in both houses of the federal parliament. His political career started in the New Brunswick legislature back in 1925. He was elected seven times in succession to the House of Commons and for three years was minister of veterans affairs.
Colonel Brooks held his political views strongly and advanced them forcefully. He was a partisan in the best sense of the term, and over 40 years of political service served only to enhance his reputation as a gentleman, a true patriot who was inspired always by the highest aspects of public duty. It may sound easy to speak in terms of 40 years of public service, but a man who gives it makes great sacrifices in his personal and family life. In the federal parliament, from the time of his election to the day of his retirement, he was a loyal and devoted spokesman for the interests of the Atlantic provinces, and he was always a patriot. There have been few men in public life from that region who deserve to receive unanimous respect and affection. Like many of you I have lost an old friend. On behalf of my colleagues and myself I wish to extend sympathy to Mrs. Brooks and the two sons.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre addressed a question to me as acting minister of manpower and immigration. I think with respect, that the question should have come to me as Minister of Labour since it relates to eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat again that I am not concerned about my hon. friend from Verdun. I am urging my hon. friends opposite quite earnestly to take the situation in hand and ensure we do not have any more of this. I do not think I need say anything more about it.
I wish to say, however, that as I indicated I welcome criticism. Generally speaking it is unfair, but unless it is made with regard to an issue such as this one I do not mind it very much. Some people contend there is nothing worse than unfair criticism. I have long believed that fair criticism is a great deal worse, and I intend to extend it now to my hon. friends opposite in connection with the budget.
What is the purpose of this budget message? Last spring the Minister of Finance presented a budget to the house in which he forecast a deficit of some $750 million. This was described by him as intending to provide a moderate and sustaining influence upon the economy. Why is he presenting an additional message now? Surely the need to sustain the economy in this way has not changed. Indeed, it is more apparent than ever that the economy requires support now. Apparently the deficit is a little larger now than the minister forecast, but so far as inflation is concerned it was as rampant then as it is now.
The stated purpose of the Minister of Finance was to meet growing expenditures and reduce the capital requirements of the market. I was a little surprised to hear that a budget message is required to meet growing expenditures because I thought the minister was working hard to curb expenditures. Of course there has been a failure to control expenditures in the current year, which have been significantly higher than the minister forecast. However, the point I want to make is that on the revenue side the minister's proposals make very little difference in the current fiscal year ending March 31, 1968. Of
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield course for the next year commencing on April 1, 1968 a budget will be presented in the spring.
The minister's proposals, as I understand them, are intended to increase the revenues of the government in the current fiscal year by some $45 million in relation to a total expenditure of nearly $10 billion. These new taxes are very heavy for those who are affected, but obviously they do not change the budgetary picture for this year very much in relation to the total picture.
Why has the minister delivered his budget message now? So far as the expenditure side is concerned, my hon. friends opposite have been dropping hints for a long time about cuts which would be made in the current fiscal year's expenditures. It is very clear from the statement made by the Minister of Finance that the expenditures in this fiscal year, far from being cut, will be higher than he had forecast. So why is this budget message being delivered now? Nothing significant is being done either on the revenue or the expenditure sides in this fiscal year. So despite all the talk opposite, this message has virtually nothing to do with the present year. Also, it imposes significant additional burdens on the Canadian taxpayers. Obviously the government is concerned about the deterioration in the confidence of Canadians in the government. It is so seriously concerned that it is determined to make at least a show that it will do better in the future.

I doubt that there has ever been anything like it in the 700-year history of parliament.
We all know the procedures followed in connection with estimates. Departments submit their estimates and generally add something to them because they know they are going to be cut. This has been my experience and I think it is the general experience. The estimates come in, somebody totals them and the Minister of Finance almost has a heart attack. The relevant figure, of course, in connection with expenditures is the amount of increase compared with other years, not the amount of cuts made in requests for expenditures.

Personally, I rate the importance of government expenditures more highly than others in this chamber might rate them and I may be inclined to draw the line at a higher level of expenditure than others would. It must be agreed that government expenditures during recent years have been rising more rapidly than revenues and the gross national product have been rising. In due course such rising expenditures must have their effect on enterprises in the country and on individuals. If the load which the country has to bear becomes too heavy it will undermine economic growth. For the future welfare of our people there must be expansion in the future of certain government services. I realize that. But it is not enough to say that a program is desirable; we must also decide what expenditures we may take on at any one time. It is proper for an opposition to concentrate its attention at any time on the level of government expenditures. I believe we may be entering upon a phase in which the chances of effective consultation are increasing. I had expected that when the Leader of the Opposition assumed his present role we would see the opposition measuring up to its responsibilities, measuring up to the expectations of the people of Canada. Perhaps, we have misread that great convention in Toronto when the present Leader of the Opposition was elected. We had thought there was going to be a change. But, I have seen no evidence of change, either in the speech the Leader of the Opposition has made this morning or in the speech he made when he charged this government with mismanagement.
It was the same speech that could have been made by anyone on his side of the house at any time in the past. It was a thoroughly traditional speech of the kind that was made by the leader of the opposition who preceded my hon. friend. The only difference was not in the content but in the manner and the manner, I must say, was

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition he commented on a statement that he had made as reported in the magazine, Executive, for November, 1967. For the record I should like to repeat what it was the Leader of the Opposition said, because in the main I agree with it and I think he does, notwithstanding his denial this morning. In response to a question he is quoted as having said:
I think that anybody who suggests that you can cut down on government spending or offer a substantial reduction in taxes isn't being very realistic. But any government can control the rate of the increase in expenditure.
The Budget-Mr. Sharp
That seemed to me to be the Leader of the Opposition speaking as a responsible politician and as one with long experience in the government of a province concerned about what are really the facts and reflecting his very great experience. Today we heard him, unfortunately it seemed to me, abandon the role of the reasonable man which becomes him very well and resort to a kind of political gamesmanship in which he is singularly unconvincing. He began by attacking the government, particularly my colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson), for revealing at this time some of the cut-backs that had been made in proposed spending. He said that this was unprecedented. As I recall his remarks he said something to the effect that this was the first time in 700 years of British parliamentary history that there had ever been a performance like this.
Why did the government resort to this unusual procedure? The Leader of the Opposition knows very well why, and so do the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). We were urged by the opposition not to talk in general terms but to give the substance of the government's cut-backs which they said they did not believe. That, fundamentally, is the reason the government put forward at this time evidence of its intention to keep within the ceiling of $10,300 million that I had announced both on motions one day and later in my budget speech. But the most flagrant inconsistency, it seemed to me, in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition lay in his attitude toward government spending. At one time he was for it; the next time he was against it. It was really quite a remarkable display of agility.
Usually we hear from an individual member of the opposition that he is in favour of some expenditure and then hear from another member that he is opposed. But there we have the Leader of the Opposition in the same speech appearing to be both for reduced government spending and in favour of more government spending. This a tribute to the skill he displayed, but I really do not believe it is a very great tribute to the intelligence of members of this house who listened most carefully to his very careful statement of the position of the Leader of the Opposition. There was a United States senator who once found himself in a similar spot. He told me what happened. He said that in

December 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Sharp his state there was a law about killing squirrels and that this was a very contentious matter. He was in a terrible spot because some of his friends were in favour of the law and some were opposed to it. He got up on the speaker's platform and said, "Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to speak to you about the squirrel law. Some of my friends are in favour of it and some are opposed to it. I have no hesitation whatever in stating my position. I am in favour of my friends."
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition in his speech was trying to appease his friends behind him whether they were in favour of greater government spending or opposed to greater government spending.

I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that the government has a responsibility for decision making. That is what governments are for. In this connection, then, I find great difficulty in understanding why the Leader of the Opposition should have complained because the government made and announces some decisions. This is another kind of inconsistency that I detected in the hon. gentleman's speech.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
But the opposition has a responsibility, too. That responsibility is to provide constructive opposition. That is what the opposition, in our parliamentary system, is supposed to do. There is a particular responsibility, of course, laid upon the Leader of the Opposition because he occupies a position of even greater responsibility than other members of the opposition. If he genuinely believes that the government is overspending, his party should at least not advocate large, additional expenditures and should applaud the government when it does that for which the opposition presses.
I listened last night when my colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) was speaking and announcing some economy measures. He announced the cut-backs the government was proposing. What did I hear from the opposition benches? Was it applause? No. I heard cries of "Shame" after almost each item. Let me ask the Leader of the Opposition some questions.

The Leader of the Opposition made representations to the government when he was premier of that province that it should spend more money, in large quantities, in the maritime provinces. Is the Leader of the Opposition in favour of reinstating the shipping subsidies? Is he in favour of the government spending large amounts of money on public works and new railways? Is he in favour of more aid to education? Is he in favour of enlarging the designated areas? Is he in favour of the federal government spending more money to solve the problems of water and air pollution? Have members of his party been advocating that there should be no abandonment of railway lines in the west? Have they been advocating that the federal government should provide no aid to western farmers, no subsidies in respect of wheat, and so on?
I ask these questions really to illustrate the point that these are projects which I think would receive wide support in the house, but the opposition cannot at one and the same time advocate that we make large cuts in our spending and advocate expenditures running into hundreds of millions of dollars.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They can.
(Mr. Sharp.]
December 8, 1967

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know they can advocate it, but it is an example of the inconsistency illustrated by the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. Let me deal with some of the other things that have been advocated by the opposition parties in connection with revenue. They have advocated-I do not blame them but this shows the inconsistency of the opposition-that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials be withdrawn to a very large extent, at the cost of the treasury. They have advocated cutting taxes in general. Indeed, I recall the position taken by the opposition parties in the debate on the main budget. It was directed against the fact that we had not reduced taxes, although we did to a minor extent. I would be more convinced by the arguments put forward by the Leader of the Opposition if they were not so inherently inconsistent. We have in this party and in this government tried to be reasonably consistent.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the Leader of the Opposition ought to try to reconcile some of his priorities before he lectures the house and the government.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is not in government yet, but he soon will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand the hon. gentleman's dilemma. He is in a difficult spot. He is criticizing a government that in large part is doing what the Leader of the Opposition would do if he were in office. This is the position in which he finds himself. At one and the same time he is criticizing the actions of the government, which he really agrees are necessary, and is suggesting that they are inappropriate to economic circumstances. This is a very difficult position for the Leader of the Opposition.
The Leader of the Opposition revealed his dilemma when he moved an amendment to the last supply motion. It was exactly the same dilemma as he faces today in making his criticism of the budget. He cannot be expected to solve this dilemma by the sort of double-talk in which he indulged today. He knows the problem because of his experience as premier of Nova Scotia. I am not criticizing what he did in that position. I recognize he was more familiar with the problems in Nova Scotia than I am. But he has stood in his place today and lectured this government on its spending. Therefore I should like to draw to the attention of the house the record of the government of Nova Scotia in some of
The Budget-Mr. Sharp the fields where there has been particular criticism from the Leader of the Opposition and the opposition parties.
The Leader of the Opposition pretends to be a model of fiscal and financial responsibility, interested in keeping down government expenditures and trying to keep civil servants under control. Therefore I think some comparisons with Nova Scotia are relevant. Let me give the figures. I have a great many here but I shall give only one. These figures relate to the public service in Nova Scotia. Between the years 1956 and 1966, a period when my hon. friend occupied the position of premier of that province, the public service of Nova Scotia, those in government employment, rose from approximately 10,300 to 14,419. This is an increase of just under 40 per cent. In the same period the number of civil servants in Canada rose from 336,000 to 361,000 approximately. This is an increase of just about 7 per cent. These are comparisons that I think should be brought to the attention of the house, because I believe that in discharging our responsibilities we are doing at least as well as did the government of Nova Scotia when the Leader of the Opposition was premier of that province.
The hon. gentleman in his speech made these broad, sweeping statements, namely, that the government of Canada had been irresponsible in its spending, that our spending has been too great, that we had employed too many civil servants. I suggest that his criticism of us is certainly not justified by the record of his administration in this field.
I recognize that he has special responsibilities, but I suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that so has the government of Canada on behalf of the people of Canada.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is time you lived up
to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was one notable gap in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. He talked about our Canadian problems as if somehow we were alone in the world. He made virtually no reference-I certainly did not hear it-to the sort of problems that are besetting the whole of the western world of which we form a part. I do not say this because I wish to blame external factors for all our problems. We have a responsibility and we intend to discharge it. I have been frank to say, perhaps more frank than most ministers of finance have been in the past, that we have some special problems which

December 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Sharp demand action from Canada and from Canadians. But the common problem that faces all of us, that faces the United States, Great Britain and many of our friends in Europe just as it faces us here in Canada, is a different kind of inflationary problem from any that we have ever seen before. In the main it is not brought about by an excess of demand.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The Leader of the Opposition spoke as though the kind of problem that I had been talking about in my budget speech was a traditional form of inflation brought about by excessive demand. But he knows, I am sure, that there are other factors at work, notably a kind of inflation psychology which finds its reflection in prices, wages and interest rates. This is what prompted the government to bring in another budget at this time. This inflation psychology, this tendency for wages and prices to go on rising, is jeopardizing the future growth and expansion not only of this country but of the western world in general.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, exactly, and of Nova Scotia. This is the problem with which we are dealing at this time, and it is difficult to cope with this new kind of inflation both here and abroad. Read the speeches of the secretary of the treasury in the United States, of the chancellor of the exchequer in Great Britain and of any other minister of finance in the world today, and you might be reading the speeches of the Minister of Einance of Canada.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, exactly, and of Nova Scotia. This problem is common throughout the world and we are trying to face it and deal with it in the proposals which I have put forward in my budget speech supplemented by the speech of the President of the Treasury Board.
When the Leader of the Opposition ran out of substantive arguments, when he found it difficult to square the circle any more, he resorted to the usual gambit of a leader of the opposition. He said that the government has lost the confidence of the people.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is not the first time that he has said this because once before he moved a motion of a similar kind. At the

time, however, he felt he was saying something new and different.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But I can assure him that on every occasion I have heard any leader of the opposition speak in the house he has always made the same sort of speech. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that he failed to make a case. All he made was as an assertion that the government has lost the confidence of the people and therefore the people should put his party in office to do the same thing better. I suggest that this is a lame argument and that we expect more from the opposition.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to have the opportunity to follow the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). When he first came into the House of Commons and in the years that have followed he has tried to sneer his way through successive budgets and debates rather than deal with the substance of the matters which he has brought forward from time to time. Today we heard him say that the reason for bringing in another budget was the fact that conditions had changed in Canada since he brought down the budget less than a year ago. Well, he can certainly say that again, because the forecast he made at that time was certainly not borne out by the circumstances that developed in the months that followed, and his budget at that time was a failure as was the one before it.
Today he spoke about the irresponsibility of the opposition and said he knew they would try to embarrass the government. I say to you, sir, that we do not have to try to embarrass the government because they are far better at embarrassing themselves. He spoke about the Conservative convention in Toronto and about the expectations of the Canadian people. I suggest that the government is afraid to assess the expectations of the people of Canada at this particular time. That has been very evident from what the Prime Minister has said on more thas one occasion. I suggest that when the time comes for the government to assess the expectations of the Canadian people they will find another disappointment on their doorstep.
However, the most interesting thing he said, in my view, was that certain factors in events which have taken place outside Canada have defeated the aims and objectives of the government. I say to you, sir, that what has happened externally has helped this
December 8, 1967

country in many respects. I refer to the Rhodesian problem and its effect on Canada's trade, and to the Middle East problem and its effect on Canada's oil sales and the boom that is taking place in the province of Alberta at the present time in oil exploration and the sales of oil. These events have helped to sustain the revenues of this country above those that the minister forecast in his last budget speech. Were it not for these events the situation in this country would be much grimmer than it is at the present time.
I am sorry to see that the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) is not in the house at present. If he is behind the curtains I wish he would come into the house because I should like to refer to his speech last night. He said then that Saskatchewan had a particular attitude with regard to minorities. I throw that charge back at him and I say that the province of Saskatchewan treats all its people on an equal basis. There was no justification for the charge he levelled against the New Democratic party which at one time formed the government of that province but which in all likelihood will not have the chance to do so again. In speaking about the stand taken by one of the New Democratic party members in the house he said:
The hon. gentleman knows that the basic philosophy behind the report of the Carter commission, as outlined by the chairman, is that we should either bring in the full report or nothing at all.
I take it this means that the government will, as usual, do nothing with regard to the taxation problems of this country. Then he went on to say:
I have a weak spot for the opposition, because they are the same old gang we have seen in the House of Commons for too long.
The hon. member has not been too long himself. There are many members on this side of the house who have been here much longer than he, and after the speech he made last night they will be here a whole lot longer.
Never before in the history of Canada has a government sought to attempt a deception so arrogant and so transparent as the one now encompassed by the mini-budget and the announcements made by the Minister of National Revenue last night. Last night we witnessed a refinement of arrogance and carelessness unequalled in parliamentary history. Parliament and the Canadian people were subjected to another of these diversionary facades which have become the trade
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden mark of the government, portraying the utter carelessness and unconcern of the Prime Minister and his government for the real problems which have developed in this nation. These problems were outlined in the first paragraph of the minister's address on November 30. As found on page 4899 of Hansard he said:
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The purpose of this statement is to present to the house the fiscal measures which the government considers necessary at this time to achieve three urgent and closely related objectives: first, to restrain the inflationary increases in prices, costs and the cost of living that are undermining our prosperity;-
This is an admission by the minister that his policies during the last two years have been wrong.
-second, to ease the disturbing strains in the capital market that threaten our continued growth; and third, to meet in a non-inflationary way the costs of continuing public programs essential to social security and long run national development.
When we take a look at the budget we do not see those things contained in it, even in light of the remainder of the minister's statement. We see here corroboration of what we knew well before. This government is bankrupt for the second time within a year and for the third time within two years. This is a record that cannot be laid at the door of any other administration in Canadian history. The desperation of the government and the extent to which the financial position of this country has declined can be measured by the fact that once again, so soon after the last tax increases, the unsatisfied appetite of the government for cash could be no longer delayed.
Yesterday, in answer to a question from this side of the house, the Minister of Finance stated that the sale of Canada savings bonds had lived up to the government's sober expectation. This statement by the minister responsible for the fiscal integrity of this nation can best be described as the kind of action one would expect from a drunken sailor on a spending spree. This is why we have this hang-over budget. This is why we have this bankrupt government reaching a greedy hand into the pockets of those who carry a dinner pail. This is why this budget cannot be described as anything but anti-labour.
This is why the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) came before us last night wringing his hands and trying with agility
5218	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden and futility to maintain the fagade presented by the Minister of Finance earlier. Last night in his opening remarks he said that the less fortunate throughout the world, and Canada, bear on the consciences of each and every one of us. I think they should bear on the consciences of hon. gentlemen opposite in view of the regard they have shown in this respect. There is nothing in the budget to deal with the housing crisis in Canada. I have here a few clippings that I have been able to get together from time to time. I should like to refer to them this afternoon. The first one is from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix and it refers to the National Housing Act interest rate. The article reads in part as follows:
If raising the ceiling on National Housing Act interest rates to 81 per cent is the only way to save Canada's housing problems, there may be little room for argument against it. But this new rate is so high as to be frightening to most buyers.
Hitherto, under various lower N.H.A. interest rates, people have complained that, by the time they have finished an ordinary 20 year mortgage, their interest payments have been as big as the cost of the house itself. At 81 per cent they will now pay more than twice the price of their property in 20 years.
I have another clipping from the Star-Phoenix of September 20, 1967. The headline reads, "Councillors Irked By Interest Rate". The reference is to the municipal council of the city of Saskatoon. The article reads:
A gloomy picture of the bond market was described at city council Monday night as aldermen debated whether to accept a purchase offer for $1,593,000 of civic debentures when the city is forced to offer 7.65 per cent interest.
Mayor S. L. Buckwold said the interest rate is the highest the city has ever been forced to pay in its history and council must be careful with expenditures or it will overburden the taxpayers.
It is interesting to note that Mayor Buckwold is an outstanding Liberal in Saskatchewan. Farther along the article reads:
He recommended acceptance of the Toronto company's offer which he termed "well in line" with the trend of the Canadian market.
Council decided to accept the offer.
Alderman C. A. Wheaton said he was very surprised that the city had received a firm offer to buy the debentures as many cities were experiencing great trouble.
"This speaks well for the city's credit rating", he said, "but we must watch our spending until the interest rate situation gets in hand."
I believe it was this government that brought into being these higher interest rates when they removed the ceiling on interest rates that banks could charge. I recall that in the dying days of the debate on that measure

DEBATES	December 8. 1967
I described the interest rate as a fluctuating one. This is exactly what it has been.
Here is another clipping from the Ottawa Citizen which refers to the housing crisis. The Globe and Mail for December 7 has a headline dealing with housing which reads, "Saskatchewan Builders Blame Mortgage Lack, High Interest For Housing Crisis". The article reads:
Saskatchewan builders are pointing to 1967 building figures to back up their claim that the shortage of mortgage money and rising interest rates are pricing families in the middle and lower income brackets out of the housing market...
The Saskatoon and Regina House Builders Associations claim 1967 starts are slightly lower than half of Saskatchewan's minimum new housing requirements of about 6,000 units annually...
They predict an acute housing shortage is likely to develop in early 1968.
The article refers to increases in the National Housing Act interest rate, which also affected the situation in Calgary and in Alberta generally. I will not take the time to read from this article the various points I was going to outline. The government was warned time after time by members of the opposition about the effect of the 11 per cent sales tax. Reference was made to this by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). In addition, there has been a discussion of the interest rate and the effect it would have on the construction industry in this country. There has been talk about parliament and about the effectiveness of parliamentary committees. This government never listens to what members of the House of Commons or the members of committees recommend. In any event, the government has ended up bankrupt three times in less than two years, even though they contended they knew it all and they were part of the establishment.
The government talks about containing the growth in the civil service. Even the minister had to admit that they have added 10,000 to 15,000 additional civil servants per year since this government came to office. It is estimated that in four years 50,000 additional civil servants have been hired by the government. This is the number of people the government needed to help govern because of the inadequacy of the representation they have here in the House of Commons. Then they talk about containing this growth at the present time and they try to call that efficiency. This is getting things done. The Minister of Finance admitted it costs more than twice as much today to govern as it did four years ago when the Conservatives were in office.
December 8, 1967
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Last night the President of the Treasury Board outlined 51 items which constituted a mirage that the government had seen and had decided to eliminate. He said that many more items fell into this category. I think he compared the situation to his wife asking for a new hat and his denying her the privilege of buying it. What the minister put before the house last night was an empty sieve with the marbles rolling on to the floor beyond the reach of anybody. Talk about Alice in Wonderland.
The government speaks about being realistic and coming to grips with the real problems facing the nation. Never before in parliamentary history were so many straw horses put up to be knocked down as the Minister of National Revenue put up last night. We should remember this when we discuss the mini-budget that is now before us for consideration.
What has this government done to reduce inflationary pressure at the present time? Not a single item in the budget speech or in the statement last night will end the inflationary spiral that has been occurring since this government took office. In announcing his tax increases the minister used a trick that he used a year or two ago when he stole corporation taxes from the future. Compared with the record of the former administration, the present administration has always been reaching into the future, taking money from the next year to use in the current year.
With regard to the agricultural situation since this government came into office, when the minister was minister of trade and commerce he disclaimed any responsibility for grain sales which, he said, were a matter for the Canadian Wheat Board. The minister not only convinced his colleagues but he also convinced his counterpart in Washington that the United States would not have to deal with Canadian ministers over the matter of wheat sales. As a consequence, competition has resulted of a kind which has put grain sales by this country in jeopardy in recent months. The farmers of western Canada are concerned about this and they know that the Minister of Finance has had a great deal to do with this situation.
Other problems which have been brought up during the course of this debate concerned turkeys, oil and pollution. The minister has indicated that there is a pollution problem. We on this side of the house thought there was a pollution problem across
The Budget-Mr. Nasserden the way. I say that kindly because not too many years ago hon. gentlemen opposite sat on this side of the house. When today I hear the call for constructive opposition I recall the type of opposition that came from this side of the house a few years ago. In this connection I also recall that the suggestions made by members of all political parties in respect of the successive budgets that were presented to the House of Commons fell on the deaf ears of the government.
One can draw only one conclusion from the economic situation in Canada today, namely, that it is the result of deliberate action taken by the government, first of all in proposing the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery which will have repercussions on the economy long after the tax has been removed and, second, in removing the ceiling on interest rates charged by the banks.

In the last two years, the Quebec government has increased the sales tax by 2 per cent; the federal government has increased it by 1 per cent. The Quebec government increased the personal income tax; the government in Ottawa did the same. The Quebec government increased the tax on certain goods, and so did Ottawa. We are the only people in the world who accept and tolerate that two different governments should have the right to tax us, very often, for the same purposes.
Our money is being grabbed from both sides. When two governments levy taxes, this entails expenditures that could be avoided if one government only managed our affairs. Let me give you a few examples, Mr. Speaker.
The federal government pays family allowances to children under 16 years of age; so does the Quebec government. Has anyone considered for a moment that this means that civil servants in Ottawa make a survey of all the children under 16, others keep the records up to date, prepare the family allowance cheques, stamp and mail them?
All this is happening in Ottawa, while other civil servants in Quebec do exactly the same thing in respect to family allowance cheques for children in Quebec. This duplicates the expenditures, since both Ottawa and Quebec have to set up a classification system, with a list of names of all children with respect to family allowances. Both governments have to have their own personnel____
which makes it twice as large-to send out family allowance cheques. In addition, two series of cheques and envelopes have to be used; Ottawa pays the postage once, and Quebec a second time. For postage costs only, the federal government expenditure for family allowances amounts to $2.2 million per year. Then, postage has to be paid again in Quebec to mail other family allowance cheques concerning the same children.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, how stupid it is to have a system under which citizens are governed by two separate administrations both doing the same thing at twice the cost, when one expense would be sufficient, just to send out family allowance cheques? Would it not be better to have only one administrative service, using only one envelope for both cheques?
The same thing goes for the Department of National Revenue.

speechtext:
Administrative duplication, duplication of funds to do exactly the same thing can be found also in other fields. For instance, the administration of the winter work program. The Quebec government has set up that department to check and see if the works have been carried out, if the men have been paid at least those who are sup-psed to work-and when Quebec has finished its inspection, the file for each municipality is sent to Ottawa where exactly the same inspection starts all over again for the same purposes. Therefore, we always pay twice. We pay twice more taxes because we have to pay for two administrative services which overlap.
Mr. Speaker, our country is the only one in the world with two ministers of health, one in Quebec and one in Ottawa; two ministers of justice, one in Quebec and one in Ottawa, who get in each other's way. In fact when Quebec citizens make representations to the federal Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) requesting an investigation into fraudulent bankruptcies for instance, the minister replies: That does not come under my jurisdiction only, it is partly the responsibility of the Quebec minister of justice. On the other hand, when Quebec citizens make representations to the provincial minister of justice, he also replies that he cannot do anything because that comes also under the jurisdiction of the federal Minister of Justice. Because there are two of them, they get in each other's way, and we are paying twice.
We are also the only ones to have two ministers of finance, two ministers of national revenue and to always have to pay in two places for exactly the same thing. We are the only country in the world to have two different civil services to do exactly the same thing. Hospital insurance is shared fifty-fifty by Ottawa and Quebec. On account of that, the government in Ottawa must provide a whole staff to operate this service and Quebec has to hire a different one to do

DEBATES	December 8. 1987
exactly the same work on behalf of the Quebec government. We are always paying twice.
The Minister of Finance finds that the civil service is increasing. How is he going to solve the problem? Well, the best way to do it, and without disturbing in any way the services, is to put an immediate stop to the dual administration and to give back to Quebec what comes under provincial jurisdiction, under the British North America Act. We have two administration levels which cost us twice the amount required, two levels of government which cause delays precisely because they do not agree all the time and are working at odds with one another.
That is why many here have come to the conclusion that we are two nations.
Since decisions are taken in two different places, responsibilities overlap and that doubles the administration costs.
Some people say that we are two nations. So we adopt two flags, the maple leaf flag and the Union Jack. We also adopt two national anthems: O Canada and God Save the Queen, because it is said we are two nations and, in that case, two national anthems are called for.
Last Saturday at the beginning of the Grey cup game, I heard on the C.B.C. French network the announcer say: And now here is our national anthem. And what did I hear? God Save the Queen, our national anthem? That was one nation's anthem. This was happening in Ottawa, in an English-speaking province. It was said that our national anthem was God Save the Queen, right on television in the presence of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson). That was said to be the national anthem of one of the two founding peoples. They talk about two peoples and they talk of national unity. How can they speak of national unity while claiming, in one and the same breath, that there are two founding nations? When there are two nations it is not a question of national unity but of international unity. If it is international unity, there are perforce two states. It is high time to recognize these facts Mr. Speaker.
Since we are on the budget, I should like to raise a point because I think that there are unnecessary expenditures in that area which the government could cut back slightly to achieve better results.
I should like to speak of the economic aspect of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river which the government could
December 8, 1937

make possible. A pamphlet has just been published in Montreal, the author teaches at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales in Montreal; he is Mr. Michel Brochu, a geographer holding doctorates in literature and natural sciences from the University of Paris. Professor Michel Brochu has studied this problem and, I believe, it is time for the Canadian government, which is supposed to have jurisdiction over the St. Lawrence to accept its responsibilities and do something on that score.
In his pamphlet on winter navigation on the St. Lawrence Professor Brochu mentions that the methods now being used by the icebreakers on the St. Lawrence, on the orders of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) are preposterous and unrealistic.
Professor Brochu says this in his booklet:
In fact, the captains of the ships can reach Montreal against their better judgment and at their own risk without the guaranteed assistance of the icebreakers. The port of Montreal remains open with guaranteed services to the ships who succeed in crossing the blockade.
As far as the government of Canada is concerned, its attitude is the following: let the St. Lawrence freeze completely between Montreal and Lake St. Peter and wait for those strange winter floods to happen and effect the southern suburbs of Montreal and which are precisely brought on by the ice cover which is allowed to form and deepen and under which millions of crystals of ice under pressure following the Lachine rapids accumulate and block the flow of water.
That is when the icebreakers, which are supposed to help prevent and control floods in the Montreal area, are dispatched from far away, from their winter quarters in Sorel or Trois-Rivieres, to fight this disaster. However, before they can get near Montreal, they have to make their way through thick ice, tens of miles long; more often than not, when they arrive in Montreal, the floods have already ebbed and the damage has been done.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
However, what Department of Transport officials are very careful not to divulge-and those experts cannot fail to know it-is that a radical solution to the flood problem in the communities south of Montreal would be, in fact, to tackle the problem, right from the start and all winter long, that is to handle the cause of the floods, the ice which covers the St. Lawrence right across, between Montreal and Trois-Rivieres. The means to do it is self-evident, given a single moment's thought: Ice must simply be prevented from forming in the navigable channel by having an ice-breaker go upstream and downstream every day as soon as the ice starts to form.
The cause being eliminated, there would no longer be any flood, but the implacable and ineluctable consequence of such a logical step would be that ocean-going vessels could go through the seaway all through the winter.
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire The most astonishing thing is that the people and the main newspapers of Montreal could have believed such a tale (the flood story). None of them saw through that subterfuge which costs Montreal millions of dollars every year.
The situation, Mr. Speaker, is well described. Ice is allowed to accumulate and when the floods begin, the icebreakers docked in Trois-Rivieres or Sorel are told: Go and do your job. More icebreakers must then be sent out because the ice is thicker; it takes them more time to reach the flooded areas and, by the time they get there, millions of dollars of damage have been caused. If the icebreakers were allowed to circulate before the ice thickens or before a layer of ice forms, the channel would always be open and there would never be any danger of flood.
Moreover, the government would spend less money because, even if the icebreakers are moored at Sorel or at Trois-Rivieres, even if they remain in their home port, the engines must be kept running to keep the ships warm. The personnel and the sailors who work on them are paid just the same; they must still be provided with room and board. Therefore the expenses are the same as if the icebreakers were making regular trips between Montreal and Trois-Rivieres.
Just a month ago, that is on November 7 last, the newspaper La Presse published an editorial in which Mr. Guy Cormier had the following to say and I quote:
Even if the government refuses to recognize officially that icebreakers have another mission apart from flood control, a realistic attitude would still require a logical organization of that control, that is by ordering ice-breakers to prevent the piling up of a heavy sheet of ice, the remote cause of destructive floods. It would be sufficient for an ice-breaker to sail downstream as soon as: the ice is set.
As Mr. Brochu wrote:	"The implacable and
inescapable consequence of that action would be that the way would be clear to ocean liners throughout winter".
How long will the government persist in keeping up appearances that fool no one, after all?
Mr. Speaker, that is taken from an editorial in La Presse. There was also an item on the editorial page of Le Devoir of November 6, 1967, practically along the same lines.
Winter navigation on the St. Lawrence would cost less than the present method of preventing flooding, because 5 or 7 ice-breakers would not be needed then to break the ice in case of flooding. In fact, three or four in constant use would be enough to prevent the ice from setting. It would cost less to the
5224	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire government and would allow all-year navigation up to the port of Montreal. It would also mean tremendous economic development all year long to the Montreal, Sorel, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city areas.
I wonder why people do not react to the facts Professor Brochu of the feole des hautes etudes commerciales explains. In his book, he seems to find an explanation for all this, and I quote a paragraph to prove it:
To say the least, it is surprising that none of the members of the Montreal area has taken up the cudgels for the cause of winter navigation up to the Montreal harbour.
None of the members for the Montreal region have done so; that is astonishing. For instance, the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) who comes from that area could become one of the champions of that cause. He could study the problem and ask the government to go into it deeply. Then, the-
The government would realize that the opening of the St. Lawrence to winter shipping is no problem, that the whole thing is settled, and that all that is needed is good will from the Department of Transport authorities.
Another member from the Montreal area who should take this matter at heart is the hon. member for Outremont-Saint-Jean (Mr. Noel). The hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Comtois), whose riding is quite close to Montreal should take interest in this also. The members from the Montreal area should raise the matter in caucus, as this is where they are supposed to do their work, and submit the question to the Minister of Transport and the proper authorities. But there is no reaction on this subject, and this is what bewilders me. Why do they not do something? Why is there not more insistence from the Montreal area members in favour of opening the seaway to winter traffic as far as Montreal?
This would allow the icebreakers to be used instead of being left at the dock. One of these at least could be freed. It could then be used to open navigation on the Saguenay.
This is what professor Brochu has to say on the subject:
The problem is as simple as the solution. We need only remember that ice forms on the Saguenay fjord from the island of St. Louis, 10 miles from the mouth of the river, to the first rapids upstream.
In other words, up to about Arvida.
Three vital ports for the economy of the province of Quebec are thus paralysed by ice: Port
[Mr. Gregoire.)
DEBATES	December 8, 1967
Alfred (which imports bauxite and exports aluminum) , Grande-Baie (export point for pulp and paper) and Chicoutimi (coastal shipping point). Therefore, in order to open the Saguenay to winter navigation, it would be enough, as for the section between Trois-Rivieres and Montreal, to break the new ice that is forming and coming from the Saguenay at the beginning of winter, and repeat the operation about once a week; this fjord would then be easily navigable all winter.
The ice would be carried away very easily by the strong tides which occur twice daily, with the help of the west and northwest winds which blow most of the winter. Another asset is the. almost complete absence of ice at the mouth of the Saguenay and off-shore during most of the winter.
Opening the mouth of the Saguenay to 1967 winter shipping is not a reckless nor a daring project.
It is purely a question of wanting to and of using very simple techniques, and it is surprising that the very active elite in the Lac St. Jean area has not yet tackled this question which could be solved immediately, and without doubt successfully, and which will bring in tens of millions of dollars in annual income.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the people of the Saguenay-Lac Saint Jean area have taken an interest in this problem and are asking for winter shipping on the Saguenay all the more because, according to Professor Brochu, it is not a reckless nor a daring project. It is simply a question of wanting to and of using very simple techniques.
The government could do two things: it could save by reducing our present needless spending and then, make rational use of the icebreakers which are idle between Trois-Rivieres and Montreal, so that one of them could be free to go up the Saguenay. It would not cost more and the whole economy of the area would develop.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
But why is it not done? Why refuse Quebec something that would not cost a cent more, since the men are there, paid and fed? The icebreakers are there, their motors running, in short everything is ready. The only thing we lack is the decision on the part of the Department of Transport to really allow for that winter navigation in the St. Lawrence.
I admit there may well be other areas in this country that would be unhappy, but then, let us make other plans in order to assist them in case they should suffer from winter navigation in the St. Lawrence. But the disadvantages would be quite trivial compared with the advantages for the economy of the entire central area of the country.
December 8, 1967

Once the winter navigation is made possible up to Montreal, Mr. Speaker, progress would not stop there. There would always be some technicians and scientists who would continue to try to find a method in order to extend winter navigation on the St. Lawrence and that is progress.
Therefore, I submit that point to the Minister of Finance and I hope that the Minister of Transport will take it under serious consideration. Unfortunately, there is not so many members from the Montreal area on whom I can rely for support in connection with that cause. I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and the hon. member for Outremont-Saint-Jean (Mr. Noel) and I ask them to exert pressure to make possible winter navigation on the St. Lawrence. Unfortunately, the others are not here; I also see the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), who could do his share in this respect.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope I have outlined the problem clearly and that everybody will understand now that as regards technology, finance, feasibility, nothing stands in the way of such an endeavour. All that remains now is the decision on the part of the Department of Transport, which will entail no extra expenditures.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by paying my personal tribute to my colleague the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) who spoke last night in this house and who, in my experience has been the strongest proponent of national unity both inside and outside the house, ever since I have had the honour to know him. I admire him for it and I believe every Canadian who has at heart one Canada can, in sincerity, honour him and those like him for their work in this direction.
As I believe hon. members know, I am not very politically oriented in this house, but I cannot let go unchallenged the remarks of the last speaker from the opposition who made reference to the support given by the members of my party to our leaders in this house. I should merely like to draw his attention to the fact that when his own leader spoke, upon introducing his motion of non-confidence in the government the other day, the first time he had made a major speech in this house, I took a personal count.
I will not trust my figures, but will merely point out that the newspapers drew attention to the fact that there were never more than 45 of his own members sitting in the house at
The Budget-Mr. Groos the time he made this speech. I think these figures speak for themselves, and I will not dwell on this any longer.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How many are there over on your side now?

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are not very many over here while I am speaking, but it is pretty hard to compete with Santa Claus, who is arriving outside for the children's party.
I should like to refer to the speech made last night by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) when he outlined in general terms the cut-backs and delays the government is proposing for the next financial year. I believe we all know that these will have to be made for the good of the country, because of the difficult financial conditions which exist in the country and in the world today, not all of which are of our own Canadian making. I accept that, although my riding will be affected as much as any other. I feel sure our people in Victoria will generally accept the cut-backs in the national interest and I will support the government in the measures they are taking.
There is one cut-back, however, which I simply deplore. It positively sickens me personally, at heart, to think that no money can be found for any federal superannuants, no matter how dire their circumstances may be. I must say here and now that I implore the minister and the government to take another look at their decision not to make any increase in the payments to superannuants next year. Surely there must be some way to help, if not all, at least those in most dire need. Let us at least do something for this group.
Last night I went to the parliamentary library to look up the steps which had been taken during the days when another government was having difficulty making its financial ends meet. You will notice, Mr. Speaker the mixture of books I have before me. In reading through the parliamentary debates of 1932 I noticed what steps had been taken.
So far as I can make out the civil servants of those days-and they comprise most of the superannuants of today-were not given a salary cut in those terms but, by the Salary Reduction Act, were required to make what was called at that time "a contribution to the welfare of Canada" of 10 per cent of their salaries across the board. It was reduced to 5 per cent for those who earned less than $1,200 a year. At the same time satutory increases were frozen. When this legislation

December 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Groos was brought forward in 1932 the government of the day called that a year of self denial. This was the way they handled the situation.
I found that the so-called year of self denial was extended from 1932 to 1933 and then to 1934. It was not until the Liberal government returned to office that the full pay cuts were restored.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a civil servant in those days whose pay was, for example, $1,200 a year and who had a $60 statutory increase coming to him in the normal course of events took a cut of $180 a year during these years. In other words the cut was 15 per cent and he accepted it. This little gimmick produced just over $8 million for the federal treasury, at the expense of the members of the civil service. I should like to remind hon. members that at that time, 1932, the income tax for a person earning $10,000 a year in Canada was $232.
In 1931, which is the closest year for which I can obtain this sort of statistic, the figures show there were 11,000 people in this country earning between $5,000 and $10,000, for a total of $76.75 million earnings, and a further 3,000 earning more than $10,000 for an additional total of $38 million earnings.
I should have thought that a more equitable method of raising an additional $8 million would have been to put a 10 per cent surcharge on those salaries. This would have hurt far less and would have produced almost $11.25 million, over $3 million more than was raised from the poor civil servants. I should like to go further and point out that the federal superannuants of today, after having suffered three years of cut-backs which most assuredly left them with no opportunity to save for their old age, were then faced during world war II with the freezing of their salaries. It is those persons who retired shortly after world war II for whom I plead today, with all the energy I possess. They should not have to beg and I am begging for them now.
I should like to make some positive contribution to this debate so, Mr. Speaker, if you will permit me I shall continue to speak about the federal superannuants of today.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member has not done so up to this point, Mr. Speaker. He has been fighting the 1935 election. I think he should get up to date and be contemporary.

out is that these people who have suffered, as they did, are entitled to our sympathy today in this house. I am very conscious of and sympathetic to the income problems of persons retired from the federal civil service and from the armed forces of Canada. I believe most members of this house know that I and others have been seeking by every means within our power to alleviate their distress. I am attempting again to explain my position and perhaps help the government come to grips with the problem by providing one possible solution.
In general, to run over the background, of course the pensioners' problem arises from the undoubted fact that over the years inflation has gnawed away at the real value of pension dollars earned and paid for while in the government service, and the pensioner in every case now faces the fact that his pension purchases less than it did when he first retired. In addition to this, he has the aggravating knowledge that his former position in the government service now pays a very considerably higher wage than it did while he held the position. Then, too, because of his age, there is a diminishing probability of his being able to obtain another position in today's labour market. Then there is the added possibility that all three conditions I have mentioned will continue.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
On the other side of the ledger, the government pensioner does have the prospect of receiving, along with all other Canadians, the old age security pension, now slowly dropping in age limit to 65 and payable at the rate of $75 a month. He knows however that he has paid his share of the cost of his pension. At the personal level, generally the government pensioner firmly believes that the government superannuation fund is growing at a rate faster than it is being used up, and therefore it would cost the country nothing if his pension were to be increased, since it could be paid for out of the growing amount in the superannuation fund.
He knows, too, that the British government has recognized its obligation to its retired civil servants and pensioners and has instituted a method of granting them increases at regular intervals as the purchasing power of the pound falls and as the cost of living goes up. Similar arrangements are in effect in the United States, and in addition I understand that retired members of their armed forces have pensions based on
December 8, 1967

the up to date pay of the rank they held when they retired. In Canada, in 1958, the government granted increases to certain federal superannuates who retired before December, 1952.
As I have said before, I have every sympathy with Canadian government pensioners and I support their cause wholeheartedly. My investigations, however, have shown me that things are not quite as they seem. First of all, while it is true that the federal superannuation fund is in fact growing, since its annual income is greater than its annual expenditures this can be quickly explained. The pension fund must grow, with the ever-increasing number of contributors, if it is to be self-supporting and be able to pay out pensions when they eventually become due. To deal with this right away, I should like to point out that I have introduced a measure in the house suggesting that the government set up a special commission to inquire into the status of the federal superannuation fund, and that on the commission there should be at least two full-time representatives of the federal superannuates national association.
I have suggested this commission because I think we should get at the truth of the matter. It should be proved or disproved once and for all, impartially, whether or not the government is making money out of the federal superannuation fund, and all persons concerned should be informed and convinced of the true state of affairs. This includes the government. Furthermore-and this is equally important to my mind-I have asked that this commission be empowered to make recommendations as to possible improvements in the organization and administration of the federal superannuation fund.
I have asked this because it is my firm belief that the federal superannuation fund as it is presently set up is not capable of coping with the problems of the twentieth century and, in particular, with the problems of inflation which are world wide these days. I think the fund could be set up in such a way that it could better deal with this state of affairs, and latter I will explain one alternative that occurs to me.
Looking at the situation from the government's point of view, I appreciate the fact that they have been earnestly seeking a solution. I discover first of all, on investigation, that some departments of the government are responsible for their own pensioners and the cost of any increases in pensions must come
The Budget-Mr. Groos from that department's annual vote. This is a complication. Second, having pursued this matter in some detail I have the unshakeable feeling that the government is somewhat reluctant to tie itself down to what I think is one fair solution-and the one recommended most frequently by the pensioners-namely a regular schedule of periodically reviewing pensions. The reluctance, if I can call it that, is perhaps because the government feels it would be stepping into an area the cost dimensions of which would be almost impossible to delineate and there would be, furthermore, built-in inflationary overtones. In simple terms the government may be of the opinion that it would be faced with future costs of unknown and possibly unmanageable proportions. In fairness to the government, I think it should be pointed out here that they have recently instituted the Canada Pension Plan, which will at least grant pensions to almost all wage earners. This plan does have built-in cost of living factor, but this does not help the present federal superannuate.
I have a plan which I believe the government should study. I believe it has merit, and it could be adopted very quickly both by the government and other employers if they feel so inclined. Over a fairly short number of years it would delineate the problem and employers, whether they be the government or others, would then be faced with costs both easy to calculate and, I think, perfectly manageable.
My plan, very roughly, calls first of all for the establishment of what I will call a government mutual investment fund, operated perhaps by a consortium of investment companies. Under my plan, the employee still in the government service would have far more control over his pension fund than he does at the moment. He now has none at all. He would then be entitled to decide for himself, at regular intervals, in what proportion his pension fund contributions are to be divided between the pension fund as it now operates-where his contributions and the matching government contributions grow at a fixed percentage rate-and the government mutual investment fund. In this computer age it should be a comparatively simple matter, say at the end of every month, to give the government employee a statement as to the value of his pension account. Then, as I have said before, he should be able to adjust the proportions almost at will to suit his needs or even his whims.

December 8, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Groos
The purpose of the government mutual investment fund would be to permit the government employee to share in the growth of the country through our industries and the development of our natural resources. The possibilities of growth in such a government mutual investment fund should go a long way toward keeping in step with inflation and the rise in the cost of living. It might even surpass it. In fact, the history of the growth of well-managed investment funds shows this to be likely. The cautious federal employee will keep all or most of his pension fund invested as at present. If he does this, he should know it will be at the risk of finding himself in exactly the same position as the federal superannuate does at the moment. The more venturesome federal employee will invest his funds more in the government mutual investment fund, and he should reap any benefits. As a result, he may well find his pension capital considerably greater than it would otherwise have been when he comes to retirement.
To pause for a moment in developing my proposition, I would point out that what happens today is that the government employee going to pension has, in effect, a government annuity purchased for him on the day of his retirement. It is a fixed amount, based in the main on his contributions and his age, and there are certain provisions for survivor benefits. Then, too, from time to time the government has to inject extra money into the fund to take care of salary increases beyond those due to normal promotion. I know this is an oversimplification and I apologize to the house for it, but I think it best describes the true situation. It is inflexible, and that is another fault I find with the present system.
Having said this, I will now proceed to my next suggestion. I believe that when a person retires from the federal civil service, the way these pension moneys are paid out should be more flexible than is now the case. I suggest that not everyone needs or wants to draw his full pension right away. If not, I do not think he should be forced to do so. Furthermore, I believe some persons may require a certain amount of capital when they retire. If so, I think they should be entitled to get it out of their pension fund. Why not? It's their money.
I believe the federal superannuate should, if he so desires, be permitted to leave all or a part of his money invested in the superannuation funds, fixed or mutual, just as long as he wants to, and if he dies while it is still

so invested it should then form a part of his estate.
I can see the plan I have outlined will not be an easy one for the government to accept, for a number of reasons. To begin with, it is still in the idea form, but in addition I can see that the Minister of Finance will be reluctant to allow the federal superannuation fund, which now contributes fairly large amounts to the government coffers, to slip from his grasp, since if this happened he would have to borrow equivalent moneys elsewhere to replace those amounts put into the government mutual investment fund. Furthermore the administration of the superannuation and the government mutual investment funds in the way I have suggested would be complicated and would require special equipment and personnel.
I feel sure, however, that none of these difficulties is insurmountable. The idea could be developed by persons with more expertise in these matters than I posses. The funds lost to the Minister of Finance can be raised for the government by other means over a suitable period of time, and the increased cost of administration can be calculated and perhaps allowed for as an operating cost chargeable to the fund.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I think the benefits from such a scheme as I have outlined would be several. First of all, most of these federal employees now "in the stream" would be able very quickly to establish control over their own pension funds. Once this is done, they would have little cause for complaint in the future if they found themselves in the income cost squeeze. Their pension income, quite largely, would have been determined by themselves. Of equal importance, however, is the fact that the government will equally quickly face a problem of known and manageable proportions in that, having removed from their direct responsibility most of the federal employees now in the government employment and those in the future, they would be left, in the main, only with those already retired. I think this is the point at which we want to arrive. The government can calculate exactly the cost of improving the financial position of this group. I feel most strongly that the government has a moral obligation to do this, at least to the point of re-establishing the pensioners' real purchasing power to the level where it was when they retired.
The government should give the lead to other employers in this respect. In fact some
December 8, 1967

companies have already surpassed the government in accepting a continuing responsibility for their retired employees.
There are unquestionably other methods by which the federal superannuation fund could be improved. If the special committee which I have suggested is set up, it should be able to consider them all and choose the best one.
My plan is not entirely new, but I have been espousing it in various ways for some time and this is the first time that I have spoken fully on it in the house. However, I see signs of similar schemes in the United States of America. I notice that in the Wall Street Journal of November 28, at page 32, there is an article written by W. M. Carley which I should like to quote in part. It reads as follows:
Major insurance companies are getting set to invade the multi-billion dollar mutual fund business.
The big insurers already have dipped into common stock investments by offering variable annuity plans in which the payments to pensioners rise and fall with the market value of the common stocks in the plan's portfolio. Most of these plans, however, are available only on a group basis.
Now, the insurers are preparing to plunge full tilt into selling mutual funds outright.
Further on, the article continues:
Conventional life insurance premums are currently invested mainly in bonds and mortgages, giving the insurance company only a fixed dollar return, the value of which can be eaten away over the years by inflation. Investments in common stocks, in contrast, provide a hedge against inflation by giving the insurance companies a chance to benefit from rising market values.
Then it goes on to say:
"Practically every major insurance company will be in the mutual fund business soon", a senior vice president for one company says. "When one goes in, the others are forced by competitive pressures to follow."
Many insurance companies already have started to sell variable annuity policies, a middle road between conventional life policies and mutual funds. Like the funds, payouts from variable annuities may fluctuate because part of their value is based on investment in common stocks. But, as with insurance policies, the payout can be guaranteed to the holder's death.
I see my time is nearly up. I put forward my suggestion in all sincerity and earnestness. I know there are many others on both sides of the house who share the same concern for the plight of the federal superannuation pensioners. I ask the minister to look into my suggestion. I do not claim it has any particular merit, nor is it particularly original, but I put it forward as one means whereby the government may be able to
The Budget-Mr. Colin Cameron resolve the present unhappy situation, and I urge the minister most sincerely to consider it.
